1135.title: Heaven's wide net
1135.hook: heaven's net is wide and loose, yet nothing slips through (Tao Te Ching 73)
1135.howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter seventy-three's wide-meshed net as a picture of a world that holds together without force, and some read it as a reminder that nothing done stays hidden.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was don't crowd them, the last of the week: give people room. Your line was give room. A new week starts now.

A fishing net hangs drying on a fence. The holes are big enough to put a fist through, and water runs straight through it. It looks like it couldn't hold anything. And yet, cast the right way, at the right depth, it comes back full. Chapter seventy-three of the Tao Te Ching hangs a net like that over the whole world. Before it gets there, it talks about two kinds of courage.
screen: `A NET WITH WIDE HOLES.` → `IT STILL COMES BACK FULL.` → `TWO KINDS OF COURAGE.`

segments.voice: First, the two kinds of courage. Bold in daring, and you're killed; bold in not daring, and you live. One brings benefit, one brings harm. Then the chapter shrugs: what heaven dislikes, who knows the reason? Even the sage finds this hard. That honesty matters; the chapter doesn't pretend the world's workings are easy to read. Second, how heaven's way works. It doesn't fight, yet it's good at winning. It doesn't speak, yet it's good at answering. It isn't summoned, yet it comes on its own. It seems slack, unhurried, yet it plans well. Every line pairs an absence with a result. Third, the net. Heaven's net is vast, its mesh is wide, and yet nothing is lost. It isn't tight; it doesn't grab or chase. Still nothing falls out of it. Readers take this a few ways: as a promise that things come back around, as reassurance that the world holds together without anyone clutching, or as a warning that nothing done is really hidden. The chapter doesn't pick. Fourth, loosening the grip. A lot of worry is an attempt to tighten the mesh: to check every thread, control every outcome, close every gap yourself. Heaven's net is a different picture: loose, patient, and holding. Not every result will be the one you want. But the clutching isn't what holds it.

segments.voice: Let the breath come and go without managing it, and bring to mind one thing you've been gripping: a result you're waiting on, a situation you keep checking. Picture it resting in a wide net, holes and all; you've done your part. When the urge to check or fix comes back, let the mesh stay loose.
Heaven's net. Chapter seventy-three: vast, wide-meshed, and yet nothing slips through. Today's word.
Your line: heaven's way holds without grabbing. Wide mesh, and nothing lost. Go gently today, and I'll see you tomorrow.

1136.title: Threatening with death
1136.hook: if people don't fear death, why threaten them with it? (Tao Te Ching 74)
1136.howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter seventy-four as a challenge to rule by fear: threats lose their force once people stop fearing them, and taking ultimate power into one's own hands harms the one who does it.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was heaven's net: wide-meshed, and yet nothing slips through. Your line was heaven's net.

If you do that one more time, there will be consequences. It gets said in kitchens, offices and classrooms. Sometimes it works. Often it buys a few hours. And sometimes it gets the reply nobody wants: go ahead. Then the threat is spent, with nothing left behind it. Chapter seventy-four of the Tao Te Ching takes that moment as far as it goes, to the threat of death itself.
screen: `ONE MORE TIME, AND...` → `GO AHEAD.` → `A SPENT THREAT.`

segments.voice: First, the question. If the people don't fear death, the chapter asks, what's the use of threatening them with death? It's addressed to rulers, and it's blunt logic: a threat only works on someone who still has something to lose. Push people far enough, and the biggest threat there is stops meaning anything. Second, the other side. Suppose people always feared death, and someone did something monstrous and could be seized and put to death. Who then would dare? It's not a call for more punishment; it shows how thin the whole strategy is. Third, the carpenter. There is, the chapter says, an executioner who does the killing, an office that belongs to it. Killing in that executioner's place is like cutting wood in place of the master carpenter, and whoever does that rarely gets away without hurting their own hand. Readers differ on who the executioner is: some say heaven, or the Tao itself; some say the proper course of things. Either way, reaching for the ultimate power over another person wounds the one who reaches. Fourth, the smaller blades. Anyone can hold them: do this or I'll leave; do this or you're off the team. The question still works at that size: what happens when the threat stops scaring them, and what does wielding it do to your own hand? And if threats at home ever leave you afraid for your safety, you don't have to carry it alone: call local emergency help, or in the US, call or text 988.
screen: `A THREAT NEEDS FEAR.` · `HOW THIN THE STRATEGY IS.` · `CUTTING FOR THE MASTER CARPENTER.` · `THE SMALLER BLADES.` · then, large: `NO THREATS.`

segments.voice: Think of one if-you-don't-then line you've used lately, out loud or only in your head, with someone else or with yourself. Hear it once more, then notice the hand that holds it, the tight jaw, the shoulders, and imagine setting it down. What could you say instead that asks, rather than warns?
Threatening with death. Chapter seventy-four: if people don't fear death, why threaten them with it? Whoever cuts in the master carpenter's place hurts their own hand. Today's word.
Your line: no threats. A plain request asks; a threat only warns. See you tomorrow.

1137.title: Why people starve
1137.hook: people starve because rulers take too much (Tao Te Ching 75)
1137.howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter seventy-five as a sharp word to anyone in power: hunger, unrest and desperation below are traced to taking, meddling and grasping above.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was threatening with death: a threat needs fear, and the hand that wields it gets cut. Your line was no threats.

A cheap T-shirt in a shopping cart. A delivery that shows up in an hour. A price that seems too good. Behind each one is a person who carried part of the cost: the stitching, the late shift, the long drive. They don't appear on the receipt. Chapter seventy-five of the Tao Te Ching reads that kind of receipt for a whole country. It looks at hungry people and answers a question that's easy to skip: who took the bread?
screen: `A PRICE TOO GOOD.` → `NOT ON THE RECEIPT.` → `WHO TOOK THE BREAD?`

segments.voice: First, the hunger. The people are starving, the chapter says, because those above them eat up too much in taxes. No talk of bad luck or lazy farmers; it points straight up the ladder. Second, the unrest. The people are hard to govern because those above are always doing things, always busy with their own plans. Trouble below is traced to busyness above. Third, the recklessness. The people take death lightly because those above chase after life too greedily. When the top grabs so hard at living, the bottom is left with so little that risking everything starts to look reasonable. Three problems, each traced to the same place. Then a quieter closing line: one who doesn't make a busy project of living is wiser than one who prizes living too dearly. Fourth, the chain. No crown is needed for this. Chains run through ordinary life too: a shopping cart, a payroll, a household, a group project. The chapter's habit is worth borrowing. When something goes wrong lower down, before asking what's wrong with them, ask what's being taken from above, and who carries it. And if life itself ever starts to feel that light to you, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, or call local emergency help.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one ordinary thing from your day: a meal, a ride, something you bought, a task someone did for you. Follow it back one step, to who made it, moved it or cleaned up after it, and let one face or one role come to mind, even someone you've never met. You don't need to fix anything; just let them be seen.
Why people starve. Chapter seventy-five: because those above take too much. Hunger, unrest and recklessness are all traced back up the chain. Today's word.
Your line: who carries it. The cost never just vanishes; someone, somewhere, holds it. That's today.

1138.title: The green twig bends
1138.hook: living things are soft and supple, dead things hard and stiff (Tao Te Ching 76)
1138.carry: the soft and yielding are companions of life
1138.howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter seventy-six as a teaching on flexibility: what is alive bends, what is dead is stiff, and rigid strength tends to break.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was why people starve: hunger traced up the chain to those who take too much. Your line was who carries it.

Try to snap a green twig on a bush, and it won't break cleanly. It bends, folds over, and hangs on by a strip of bark. Now try a dead stick from the ground: one quick crack, and it's two pieces. Same plant, maybe, same thickness. The difference is that one is alive. Chapter seventy-six of the Tao Te Ching builds a whole teaching on that crack, starting not with plants but with the human body.
screen: `A GREEN TWIG BENDS.` → `A DEAD STICK CRACKS.` → `THE DIFFERENCE IS LIFE.`

segments.voice: First, the body. When people are born, the chapter says, they're soft and supple; when they die, they're hard and stiff. That's not a metaphor yet. It's just what a body does. Second, the plants. Grass and trees, alive, are soft and tender; dead, they're dry and brittle. The two pictures sit side by side so the pattern is hard to miss. Third, the conclusion. So the hard and the stiff are companions of death, it says, and the soft and the yielding are companions of life. Then the pattern moves into the world of power: an army that's too rigid doesn't win, and a tree that's too stiff meets the axe. The big and hard end up below; the soft and supple end up above. That reverses what force usually expects. Fourth, can it still bend? Stiffness shows up in more than joints: a position held so hard there's no room to hear anything, a routine that can't bend for a sick kid, a jaw clenched through a whole meeting. The chapter's test is simple. If something can't bend, it may be less alive than it looks. Soft, here, doesn't mean giving up. The green twig still holds. It just holds by bending.
screen: `BORN SOFT, DIE STIFF.` · `GREEN PLANTS, DRY PLANTS.` · `STIFF TREES MEET THE AXE.` · `CAN IT STILL BEND?` · then, large: `SOFT IS ALIVE.`

segments.voice: Seated or standing, let the breath lead: on an in-breath, lift the arms or roll the shoulders slowly, and on the out-breath, let them soften. Find one place that's holding stiff, maybe the jaw, the hands, the lower back, and breathe toward it until it gives a little. Stay within what feels easy; nothing here is a contest.
Soft is alive. Chapter seventy-six: living things are soft and supple, dead things hard and stiff; the soft are companions of life. Today's word.
Your line: the soft and yielding are companions of life. Bending isn't breaking. Rest well, and I'll see you tomorrow.

1139.title: Stringing a bow
1139.hook: heaven's way is like stringing a bow: it lowers the high and raises the low (Tao Te Ching 77)
1139.howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter seventy-seven's bow as a picture of balance: heaven's way takes from excess to supply lack, and the sage gives from surplus without claiming credit.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was soft is alive: the green twig bends, the dead stick cracks. Your line was soft is alive.

To string a bow, an archer braces one tip against the ground and bends the wood. The top comes down, the bottom comes up, the string slips into its notch, and suddenly a curved stick is a tool with tension and balance from end to end. It's a small, practical motion, done without thinking. Chapter seventy-seven of the Tao Te Ching watches it and says: that's how heaven works.
screen: `BRACE AND BEND.` → `TOP DOWN, BOTTOM UP.` → `THAT'S HOW HEAVEN WORKS.`

segments.voice: First, the bow. Isn't heaven's way like stringing a bow? the chapter asks. What's high is pressed down; what's low is lifted up. Readers picture it two ways: bending the bow to string it, or adjusting the string so the aim comes true. Either way, the motion evens things out. Second, the rule, said plainly: heaven's way takes from what has too much and gives to what has too little. Third, the contrast. The way of people, the chapter goes on, isn't like that. It takes from those who don't have enough to give to those who already have too much. Then a question: who can take what they have in excess and offer it to the world? Only someone who has the Tao. The chapter doesn't soften this. It sets heaven's way and the human habit side by side and lets the gap speak. Fourth, the sage, who acts without holding on, finishes the work without staying to claim it, and has no wish to show off his worth. That's giving from the top of the bow done well: quietly, without a plaque. Day to day, it's less about grand charity than about noticing where things have piled up in your own life, extra time, extra chairs, extra coats in the closet, extra patience on a good day, and where, nearby, something is running low.
screen: `HEAVEN BENDS LIKE A BOW.` · `TAKE FROM TOO MUCH, GIVE TO TOO LITTLE.` · `THE HUMAN HABIT RUNS BACKWARD.` · `GIVE WITHOUT CLAIMING.` · then, large: `LOWER THE HIGH.`

segments.voice: Let the breath even out, like a bow finding balance, and take a quiet inventory of what you have more of than you use: things, yes, but also time, skill, attention, a spare room, a kind word. Then let one person or place come to mind that's running short of exactly that. Hold the two together, the high and the low, and let a small way to bring them level take shape.
Stringing a bow. Chapter seventy-seven: heaven's way presses down the high and lifts the low, taking from too much to give to too little. Today's word.
Your line: lower the high. Heaven's way evens things out, from too much to too little. Rest well.

1140.title: Nothing softer than water
1140.hook: nothing is softer than water, yet nothing beats it for wearing down the hard (Tao Te Ching 78)
1140.tomorrow: keep your half of the tally
1140.howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter seventy-eight's water as a picture of gentle persistence: the soft wears down the hard, and the one who takes on what others won't is the one fit to lead.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was stringing a bow: heaven's way presses down the high and lifts the low. Your line was lower the high.

Pick a stone out of a streambed and turn it over in your hand. It's smooth and rounded, with no sharp edge left. Nobody sanded it or hammered it. The stream did that, flowing over and around it, season after season. Water never pushed hard on that stone; it just never stopped. Back on day one thousand thirty-nine, chapter eight likened the highest excellence to water. Chapter seventy-eight of the Tao Te Ching looks at water's quiet winning, and then admits something uncomfortable.
screen: `A STONE FROM THE STREAM.` → `NOBODY SANDED IT.` → `IT JUST NEVER STOPPED.`

segments.voice: First, the claim. Nothing under heaven is softer or weaker than water, the chapter says, yet for wearing down what's hard and strong, nothing does better; nothing can take its place. Water doesn't win by becoming hard. It wins by staying water. Second, the admission. The weak overcomes the strong, the soft overcomes the hard. There's no one in the world who doesn't know this, the chapter says, and no one who can put it into practice. That's honest: the lesson isn't hidden, just hard to live. When pushed, the reflex is to push back harder. Third, the sage's saying. Whoever takes on the dirt of the country is fit to tend its altars; whoever takes on its misfortunes is fit to rule under heaven. Like water, which flows to the low, dirty places and carries what others won't, the one who leads is the one who absorbs. Fourth, the last line: straight words seem backward. Some readers hear the whole book in it. Soft wins. Low leads. Giving keeps. It sounds upside down, and the chapter knows it. Day to day, water's way is persistence without force: practicing the hard piece for a few minutes each day instead of attacking it once, showing up kindly to the same difficult person again, saying the true thing gently, and again next week.

segments.voice: Let the breath move like water, without effort, just continuing, and bring to mind one hard thing you've been pushing against: a skill, a habit, a stuck conversation. Instead of a big push, think of the stream on the stone, and find one small, gentle thing you could do toward it, almost too small. Rest with the feeling of slow, steady pressure that doesn't strain.
Nothing softer than water. Chapter seventy-eight: nothing is softer, yet nothing beats it for wearing down the hard. Today's word.
Your line: water wins. It never pushes hard, and it never stops. Tomorrow: keep your half of the tally.

1141.title: Keep your half of the tally
1141.word: Keep your half of the tally
1141.hook: after a great quarrel, some resentment stays; the sage keeps his side of the tally and demands nothing (Tao Te Ching 79)
1141.howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter seventy-nine as advice on old grievances: settling a great resentment leaves some behind, so the sage keeps his side of an agreement and does not press others for what they owe.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was nothing softer than water: the softest thing wears down the hard by never stopping. Your line was water wins.

The fight is over. Apologies were said, maybe even hugs, and everyone agreed to move on. Then, a month later, a small remark lands wrong, and there it is again: the old sting, right where it was. Making peace and being at peace are two different things. Chapter seventy-nine of the Tao Te Ching starts there, with what's left over after the treaty is signed. Its first line came up on day nine hundred ninety, about reconciling; today the chapter goes further.
screen: `THE FIGHT IS OVER.` → `THE STING IS STILL THERE.` → `WHAT'S LEFT OVER.`

segments.voice: First, the leftover. When a great resentment is settled, the chapter says, some resentment is sure to remain. How can that be called good? Patching things up after a big break doesn't get everything back. Better, the chapter implies, not to pile up the debt in the first place. Second, the tally. A tally, as commentators describe it, is a record of an agreement split into two halves, one for each side, so the halves can be matched later. The sage holds his half and makes no demands on the other person. He has the proof; he just doesn't press it. Third, two kinds of people. Those with virtue look after the tally; those without it look after collecting. One keeps the agreement and lets it rest. The other is always out knocking on doors for what's owed. Fourth, the last line: heaven's way has no favorites, and it is always with the good person. That pulls the week's thread tight. Heaven's net is loose but loses nothing. Threats wound the one who holds them. Hunger traces back to those who take too much. Soft is alive. The bow lowers the high. Water wins by never forcing. And today: hold your half, and don't collect. It looks like knowing exactly what someone owes you, and choosing not to send the bill.
screen: `SOME RESENTMENT REMAINS.` · `THE SAGE HOLDS HIS HALF.` · `KEEP THE TALLY, DON'T COLLECT.` · `A WEEK OF NOT FORCING.` · then, large: `DEMAND NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you've been waiting for someone to give you: an apology, a thank-you, a favor returned, money owed. You may well be right that it's owed; hold your half of the tally, the knowledge of it, and for these two minutes set the demand down beside you. Notice what the hands, the chest and the jaw do when you stop collecting.
Keep your half of the tally. Chapter seventy-nine: the sage holds his half of the agreement and makes no demands on the other. Today's word.
